title: Hypothesis-driven Observability Triage Playbook
author: Liam Chen
body:
Overview

This playbook defines a hypothesis-driven approach to platform observability triage. It is intended for platform operators, SREs, and on-call engineers who investigate degradation in Redwood's inference runtime, routing, and tenant-facing services. The goal is to reduce mean time to insight (MTTI) by focusing investigation effort on the highest-probability causes, linking dashboards and signals to explicit hypotheses, and tracking hypothesis outcomes for continuous improvement.

When to use this playbook

- Tail latency spikes, cost-surges, or multi-tenant quality regressions not immediately explained by a single alert.
- Partial-region degradations or asymmetric tenant impact where root cause is unclear.
- Post-incident analysis for recurring failure classes that lack clear instrumentation.

Quick summary

1) Form a concise hypothesis (1 sentence) that maps symptoms to a likely subsystem.
2) Execute a prioritized signal checklist that tests the hypothesis.
3) Triangulate with related dashboards and span traces.
4) Decide: mitigate, roll back, throttle, or escalate.
5) Record the hypothesis outcome and update the catalog.

Hypothesis format (required)

- "When [symptom], then [suspected subsystem / cause] because [evidence anchor]."
- Example: "When global generate latency P95 > 750ms and only model-x tenants are affected, then KV-cache sharding imbalance on model-x is suspected because CPU and IPC for cache-shard-3 are >80% while other shards sit idle."

Investigation checklist (ordered by signal cost / speed)

1) Surface: confirm the symptom with a lightweight SLI query (<=30s).
   - Datadog (approx): timeseries query: avg(last_5m):p95(request.latency){env:prod} by {region,model_variant}
   - PromQL (approx): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le,region,model))
2) Scope: determine blast radius (tenant count, regions, models). Use tenant heatmap dashboard.
3) Resource signals: check per-GPU CPU, GPU utilization, memory pressure, and nvlink errors.
4) Runtime signals: KV cache hit ratio, batch fill times, continuous-batching queue depth, and prefix cache eviction spikes.
5) Network signals: egress latencies to model-storage (S3/R2), packet drop rates, and inter-node RPC latencies.
6) Recent changes: check rollout notebooks, canary results, infra deploys, config updates in last 60 minutes.
7) Dependency: third-party model serving tiers (if using a remote variant), container runtime OOMs, or kernel logs.

Signal-to-hypothesis mappings (examples)

- Symptom: Single-model P95 increase + per-shard CPU hot spot
  - Hypothesis: KV-cache shard hotspot or shard mapping drift
  - Signals: cache-shard CPU, cache hit ratio per shard, cache-eviction rate, recent shard rebalances

- Symptom: Region-wide tail-latency with normal per-node CPU
  - Hypothesis: Network flapping / inter-region congestion or a noisy edge prefetch layer
  - Signals: inter-node RPC latency percentiles, BGP/route changes (if available), edge-prefetch queue backlog

- Symptom: Token-cost spikes without latency increase
  - Hypothesis: model variant regression causing higher token usage (prompt expansion or sampling change)
  - Signals: token-count per-request histogram, rollout index for model variants, LLMeval quality metric drift

Decision matrix (operator actions)

- If SLO burn < 1% in last hour: continue monitoring + run targeted mitigations (soft-throttle, cache prefetch hint).
- If SLO burn 1–5% or rising: apply mitigations (route to fallback model-variant, increase batch size for cheap models) and notify owners.
- If SLO burn >5% or customer-visible failures: escalate to incident channel, consider regional traffic evacuation and emergency model swap.

Example runbook steps (for cache-shard hotspot hypothesis)

1) Validate: confirm shard CPU > 70% and hit ratio drop > 10% vs 1h baseline.
2) Short mitigation (<= 10 min): enable per-tenant rate-limiter for highest-traffic tenants on shard, reduce batch-size target for shard to spread scheduling.
3) Mid mitigation (10–60 min): trigger on-demand shard rebalancer with conservative migration throttle; if unavailable, route new traffic away from affected shard via routing policy (canary flag: route-avoid-shard).
4) Fallback: if mitigations fail, swap to model-variant with lower KV pressure (model-x-quant4) and raise incident.
5) Postmortem: capture hypothesis outcome and update hypothesis catalog entry.

Example alert rules and sensible thresholds

- Alert: inference_tail_latency_p95_high
  - Query: p95(request.latency) by (region,model_variant)
  - Condition: p95 > 750ms for 3m
  - Priority: P2
  - Runbook: follow hypothesis checklist -> scope -> resource signals -> mitigation

- Alert: cache_shard_cpu_hotspot
  - Query: avg_over_time(cache_shard_cpu_percent[2m]) by (shard) > 70
  - Priority: P3
  - Runbook: run cache-shard hotspot steps above

- Alert: token_cost_surge
  - Query: rate(tokens_processed_total[5m]) / rate(requests_total[5m]) increase > 1.4x vs 1h baseline
  - Priority: P2
  - Runbook: check recent model rollouts and prompt transformations; if confirmed, roll back variant.

SLO and impact estimation table (quick reference)

| Symptom class | Immediate SLO impact (1h) | Suggested operator blast radius check |
|---------------|---------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Tail latency spike (region) | 0.5–3% | region, tenant percentile, model variant |
| Token cost surge | 0.1–2% (cost) | token histogram, model rollout index |
| Partial-model regression | 0.2–4% | tenant mapping, cache shard maps |

Ownership and channels

- Primary on-call: Platform Operators (rotation: platform-operators@redwood.com)
- Secondary escalation: Serving Runtime (serving-runtime@redwood.com)
- Product/Customer impact: Customer Success for affected tenants (cs-alerts@redwood.com)

Hypothesis catalog and feedback loop (continuous improvement)

1) After every triage, record: hypothesis statement, signals checked, chosen mitigation, time-to-mitigation, and final outcome.
2) Monthly review: SRE lead and runtime engineers run the catalog to identify frequent failure classes and missing signals.
3) Instrumentation priorities: add metrics that would have reduced MTTI for top-5 recurring hypotheses.

Onboarding checklist for new platform operators

- Read: this playbook and the platform operator quick-reference.
- Practice: run three synthetic triage drills in the platform lab (see /eng-platform/team-wiki/platform-lab-governance-and-synthetic-workload-seeding-policy-2024).
- Verify: you can run the example queries and understand model variant tags and shard topology.

Maintenance and governance

- Catalog owner: Observability Working Group (OWG) - meets weekly.
- Update cadence: hypothesis catalog entries must be reviewed quarterly or after any incident where they were applied.
- Dashboard hygiene: dashboards referenced by cataloges should have explicit author and last-updated meta (>owner, last_updated tag).

Appendices

A. Useful queries and snippets
   - Datadog: avg(last_5m):max:request.latency{env:prod,region:us-east-1,model_variant:model-x}.rollup(max,60)
   - PromQL: sum by (shard)(rate(cache_evictions_total[5m])) / sum by (shard)(rate(cache_access_total[5m]))
   - SQL: SELECT tenant_id, count(*) as requests, percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) as p95 FROM inference_requests WHERE ts > now() - interval '10 minutes' GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY requests DESC LIMIT 20;

B. Recommended instrumentation additions (top-5 backlog items)
   - Per-shard cache hit ratio with 1m granularity
   - Tenant-level token histogram (p50,p90,p95,p99)
   - Batch fill latency broken out by model_variant and tenant_tier
   - Inter-node RPC p99 with sampling of slow traces
   - Edge-prefetch queue depth with tenant attribution

C. Postmortem template fields (add to incident packet)
   - Symptom,
   - Hypotheses tested (ordered),
   - Signals observed,
   - Mitigations attempted and time windows,
   - Final resolution,
   - Instrumentation gaps and action items.

Contact and references
